newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean stocks surge in relief as strikes end.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean stocks surge in relief as strikes end.

text.p: South Korean stocks jumped more than three percent on Monday in apparent relief the country is heading back to work after weeks of strikes and on hopes that a new labour law could lift the sagging economy.
But economists cautioned that even though a peaceful end to industrial unrest was in sight, the export-led economy faced wrenching problems.
The immediate signal to buy was an announcement that President Kim Young-sam had agreed to meet opposition leaders to try to defuse an industrial crisis sparked by passage of a new labour law.
The bill aims to trim industrial costs by making it easier for firms to lay off workers. Steeply rising wages unmatched by productivity gains have eroded South Korea's competitive edge.

The leading stock index surged 3.49 percent to 718.46. Bargain-hunting had set in even before the announcement and the index is now up 10 percent on the year after shedding 26 percent of its value last year.
By the close of trading on Monday, foreign investors had bought a net 249.7 billion won ($294 million) worth of stocks so far this month, up from 55.8 billion won in December.
Foreigners were piling back into the market because it was seen as oversold, not because they believed that an end to the strikes meant the economy was back on track, analysts said.
Factories returned to full production after the militant Korean Confederation of Trade Unions ended indefinite strikes and limited stoppages to once a week on Wednesdays.
Economists said they believed the new law would tame militant unions and lead to greater efficiencies.
"Heavy industries, such as auto making and shipbuilding, have traditionally had strong labour voices," said Yeo Kyung-ho, head of research at Daewoo Securities.
Figures released on Monday showed production losses from more than three weeks of wildcat strikes were expected to reach more than $3 billion. Export losses were put at $483 million.
"We're moving very cautiously, like stepping on ice," said Yoon Park, investment manager at Prudential Portfolio Managers in Hong Kong.
"Any resolution of the strikes isn't going to resolve Korea's economic problems," said Jonathon Dutton, an analyst at SBC Warburg in Seoul.
He said slowing growth and a ballooning balance of payments deficit largely reflected falling prices for major export items, especially semiconductors.

"One way in the long run to improve labour competitiveness is to make the workforce more flexible and increase the downward pressure on wages. So long term, the law is positive, and encouragingly the Koreans have decided to tackle the problem," Dutton said. Park said labour reform was "an unexpected gift to the stock market" by giving beleaguered corporations a better grip on costs as their export earnings plummet.
"Once Korean companies have flexibility to control costs, they can improve their bottom lines," Park said.
Brokers said a breakthrough on the strikes was timed perfectly to take advantage of a surge of funds from heated U.S. investors looking for bargains in emerging markets.
"Korea was the first economy in Asia to really dip down, and as such could be among the first to dip up," said Daniel Harwood, regional director at HG Asia in Seoul.
"There is a general feeling that the market was oversold, so people are happy to invest. They see value here."
